title: Can we automatically generate quiz questions from textbooks？ - ACL 2022 Short Paper Talk

transcript.text: Hello, in this short talk, I'd like to convince you of the following three things.
One, that summary is improved question generation.
Two, that the upper bound of the performance improvement achievable from using
summaries is quite high.
And three, that current question generation models are good enough to be used in
classroom settings today.
What is our paper about?
So this project came from the fact that my advisor had to teach a class full of
students and they gave us feedback to improve the readie quizzes.
And my advisor thought, can we automate this?
And so we did.
Our idea was we took the textbook.
Extract the text from the textbook, pass it through a model that generates
questions.
And then we would have questions that we could then filter to create our reading
quizzes from.
In order to do this, we needed to get a question generation model.
And so we looked on the Hugging Face model hub and found this great model
trained by Siraj Patil, who is a Hugging Face engineer.
This model was trained on three different pre-training tasks.
First, answer extraction, then answer where question generation.
And finally question answering.
We evaluated this model's output by asking our annotators to annotate each
question for five points.
One is, would you directly use this question in a quiz?
Two and five are the standard grammaticality and correctness questions.
And the three and four are, does the question make sense out of context?
And is this question relevant?
We found that while grammaticality and correctness were very high, we struggled
to get relevant and interpretable questions.
And this resulted in only one of three questions being actually acceptable
to use in the quizzes.
So let's look at this a little bit further.
So an uninterpretable question is one that you can't make sense of out of context.
So what seems to matter more than its frequency?
We don't know what it is.
It's uninterpretable.
For relevant questions, something like what do algorithms have to deal with?
Ambiguities.
It's a well-formed question, but it's not something you'd want on your quiz
because it actually just doesn't matter for computation linguistics.
So how do we fix this?
So our solution was to add automatic summarization.
So if you pass text from the textbook through automatic summarization
and then give it to a question generation model, you're only going to get
relevant questions.
Summarization model works by taking in a passage
and outputting a passage that has the same content but less words.
Note that it's extracts only the most relevant sentences.
So if we do this, we actually get a huge improvement.
So we see improvements in interpretability, huge improvements in relevance
and this corresponds with 50% now.
So one and two questions being acceptable.
But summarization sometimes makes mistakes.
So this passage is completely nonsensical that came out of the summarization model.
How do we know what the upper bound on performance is for summaries if they were perfect?
If we compare to human written summaries, we can see what would happen if we had
perfect summaries that would never mess up.
We compare to human written summaries and we're very surprised to see that we had
over 90% interpretable questions, over 90% relevant questions, and we had
four out of five questions as directly acceptable.
I hope I've convinced you of the following.
Summarization improves QG.
Upper bound on performance is very high and QG models are usable in classrooms today.
What more detail? Read the paper.
Want to run the code? Check out our GitHub.
And thanks so much to my awesome collaborators and thank you for listening.
